steps.reason: full_name is personal data and unique per employee. department_name repeats department one to one. date_first_hired is a date stored as text that no step can parse, and year_first_hired holds the same information. 2016_gross_pay_received is what the employee was paid for the salary being predicted (correlation 0.89), so it would leak the target.
The target is continuous, so there are no classes to stratify on; a seeded random 80/20 split keeps the run reproducible.
17 genders are missing; the most frequent value is a safe fill for so few rows.

88% of the values are missing, and the missing value means the employee holds the title they were hired for; a value means they are temporarily in a lower title. The two groups differ in pay (median 73,296 against 53,788), so the fact is kept as the category 'None'.

32% are missing while only 6 rows hold an explicit 0, so a missing overtime pay evidently means no overtime and the fill is 0. The indicator is kept because the missing values are concentrated in a few departments (all of ZAH, 7% of DLC) and the rows with a missing value have a higher median salary, which fits departments that do not record overtime.
Text categories with two to 37 values; one-hot is the family-neutral encoding.
694 divisions; the 50 most frequent cover 47% of the rows and the rest are grouped.
385 position titles and the position is the strongest signal for pay, so the 100 most frequent are kept (88% of the rows) and the rest are grouped.
Only 84 titles, and the column is mostly 'None'; the 10 most frequent are kept and the rest are grouped to avoid near-empty columns.
Overtime pay is skewed with many outliers. The model family is open and may include linear models; scaling costs trees nothing and puts linear models on comparable footing.
